description_ru: Выдуманная новость о стране, где правительство ввело ежедневную «читательскую стипендию», и о бюрократических и комических последствиях.
text:
HALDERSTOWN, Republic of Varnia. In a measure that has been variously described as visionary, absurd and "a delightful way to lose an election," the Varnian Parliament voted late on Thursday night to pay every adult citizen a small daily stipend for reading books. The Literacy Dividend Act, which passed by a margin of ninety-one votes to eighty-eight after eleven hours of debate and an unscheduled intermission for soup, will come into force on the first of March and is expected to cost the exchequer roughly the same as a modest war.

The legislation, introduced by the Minister for Culture, Beatrix Oyelaran-Finch, offers four Varnian crowns per day to any citizen who can demonstrate that he or she has read for at least thirty minutes. "For two generations we have paid people to stare at screens, and nobody was surprised when they became extremely good at it," the minister told a crowded press gallery. "We now propose to pay them to look at paper. It is a radical experiment, and I would remind honourable members that the alternative is another report on declining attention spans."

Opposition benches, as one would expect, were scandalised. The leader of the Conservative Union, Ambrose Kettlewell-Duarte, declared the policy "a bribe to the idle, delivered in the costume of virtue," and warned the chamber that the republic's tradition of self-reliance would not survive the introduction of a salary for lying on a sofa. "A citizen who requires a subsidy to read," he thundered, "is a citizen who has already lost the plot." The remark was generally considered clever, until a colleague pointed out that it was also, in a literal sense, a literary criticism.

The central difficulty, which the Act addresses with more optimism than precision, is verification. How, a sceptical Treasury official enquired, is a government to confirm that a person has genuinely read something, rather than merely holding it upside down for thirty minutes? The solution devised by the ministry is the Reading Passport, a small booklet in which citizens collect stamps from licensed Verification Librarians, who are empowered to conduct brief and, the ministry promises, "entirely non-hostile" conversations about what has been read.

Within days of the announcement, an alarming black market emerged. In the port of Kessling, police arrested a ring of forgers who had been selling counterfeit stamps at a premium, and a retired bookbinder, aged sixty-four, was caught producing convincing replicas of the Librarians' seal in his garden shed. "I did it for the craft," he told the court, with dignity. "Nobody has asked me to make anything so well in thirty years." The magistrate, visibly moved, sentenced him to a hundred hours of community service, to be served as a librarian.

The most vivid effects, however, have been cultural. Bookshops across Varnia report that sales have trebled, and that customers, who previously asked for "something quick," are now requesting "something long, because the stipend is by the hour." The publishing house of Wexcombe & Daughters has announced a tenfold increase in its demand for Victorian novels, and the great Varnian epic, The Interminable Marsh, a nine-hundred-page poem about a damp field, has returned to the bestseller lists for the first time since its publication in 1887.

Not everyone is gratified. Several authors have expressed misgivings at the spectacle of their work being consumed for money, as if it were a medical trial. The novelist Torvald Eskerley-Banda, whose latest book is described by critics as "dense, unforgiving and occasionally in Latin," observed that he had never before been read by anyone who was not under contractual obligation. "I am delighted," he said. "But I cannot help noticing that they all look rather resentful, like people eating their vegetables."

The thorniest controversy concerns what counts as reading. The Act defines it as "the sustained perusal of printed or written text," a formula that has prompted a flood of complaints. Cookery enthusiasts want recipes included; motorists wish to claim for the manual of a dishwasher; and one deputy, a keen angler, has insisted on the inclusion of the small print on a fishing licence. The ministry has issued guidelines that exclude road signs, receipts, advertising hoardings and "anything whose author is trying to sell the reader an extended warranty."

Economists, meanwhile, are scrambling to model the consequences. Dr Philippa Nwosu-Lindqvist, of the University of Halderstown, has calculated that the stipend, if consistently claimed, would amount to roughly fifteen hundred crowns a year for each citizen, a sum large enough to alter behaviour but too small to buy a decent armchair. "The paradox," she remarked, "is that the subsidy pays people to do something that is, in itself, a pleasure. It is rather like paying them to be on holiday and then asking for receipts."

There is a faint hope, shared quietly by many members, that the scheme may achieve something more subtle than literacy statistics. A pilot study in the northern district of Orsk, conducted last autumn on four hundred volunteers, found that participants who read daily for three months reported lower stress, better sleep and a markedly reduced appetite for shouting at the radio. The local police chief added that the crime rate in the district had fallen slightly, which he attributed to the fact that "burglars, too, have got to finish the chapter."

Early signs of public enthusiasm have been, by the standards of Varnian politics, almost suspicious. A queue of four hundred people formed outside the central library on Friday morning, and a spokeswoman noted that many were carrying their own chairs.

The Act is expected to face a constitutional challenge from the Association of Television Broadcasters, which has described it as "unfair competition from an inferior medium that has been available for five centuries." In the meantime, Minister Oyelaran-Finch remains serenely confident. "If history teaches us anything," she said, closing her notes, "it is that a nation which reads is difficult to govern, and thus a nation worth governing." She then paused, smiled, and added that she had a stamp to collect. The chamber, to general surprise, applauded, and several members were observed leaving the building with paperbacks under their arms, as if concealing contraband.

questions.question: What does the Literacy Dividend Act pay citizens to do?
questions.answer: To read for at least thirty minutes a day.

questions.question: How do citizens prove that they have read?
questions.answer: With a Reading Passport stamped by Verification Librarians.

questions.question: What happened to the retired bookbinder?
questions.answer: He forged the librarians' seals and was sentenced to community service as a librarian.

questions.question: What did the pilot study in Orsk find?
questions.answer: Readers had lower stress and slept better.
